title: NAT, firewalls, CDNs and curl -v
summary: Why your laptop can't be reached, what a firewall rule matches, and how to see every step of a request.

steps.title: CIDR and subnets
body: `10.0.4.0/24` means "the first 24 bits are the network": the mask is `255.255.255.0`, so the block is `10.0.4.0` to `10.0.4.255` (256 addresses).
An address is **in** a block when `(ip & mask) == (network & mask)`. Cloud VPCs, firewall rules and Kubernetes all speak CIDR.

steps.prompt: How many addresses does each block hold? This program computes `2^(32 - prefix)`.
steps.explain: Each bit you remove from the prefix doubles the block.

steps.title: NAT
body: Your home has one public IPv4 address; every device inside has a private one. The router does **NAT** (network address translation):
Consequence: outbound connections just work, but **nobody outside can start a connection to your laptop** unless you add a port-forward.
Cloud "NAT gateways" do the same for private subnets.

steps.prompt: A webhook provider must call `http://192.168.1.20:5000/hook` on your home laptop and can't connect. Why?
options: It's a private address behind NAT; nothing outside can start a connection to it without a port-forward or tunnel
steps.explain: Use a tunnel (or a port-forward to a public IP) for local webhook testing.

steps.title: Firewalls
body: A firewall (security group, NSG, `iptables`/`nftables`) checks each new connection against **ordered rules**; the first match wins, and there's a default at the end:
**Stateful** firewalls automatically allow replies to connections that were allowed out, so you write rules only for who may *start* connections.

steps.prompt: SSH to a cloud VM works from the office but times out from home. The security group allows tcp 22 from `10.0.0.0/8` and `198.51.100.0/24` (the office). Cause?
options: Your home public IP isn't in any allowed range; the firewall silently drops the SYN
steps.explain: A timeout (no reply) is the firewall signature. A wrong key would connect and then say *Permission denied (publickey)*.

steps.title: CDNs and curl -v
body: A **CDN** runs edge servers near users. DNS (often a CNAME to the CDN) sends users to the nearest edge, which serves cached copies and fetches misses from your **origin**.
Response headers like `Age: 120` and `X-Cache: HIT` tell you it came from the edge.
`curl -v` shows every layer of a request, which makes it the first debugging tool to reach for:
* SSL connection using TLSv1.3 / TLS_AES_128_GCM_SHA256   TLS
